source.title: From FusHa to Folk: Exploring Cross-Lingual Transfer in Arabic Language Models
source.authors: Abdulmuizz Khalak; Abderrahmane Issam; Gerasimos Spanakis

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures CKA similarity between Arabic MSA and dialect models and reports that alignment is incomplete and varies by input scenario and model/data scale. This refines the scope of convergence, but it does not test convergence across a controlled scale sweep or across modalities.
record.gate_note: The paper reports probing F1 results for POS, NER, and sentiment analysis, but those are task-performance measures rather than representational-distance measures named by the claim versions, so they are not rows. The CKA results are shown in figures without numerical values in the text; individual values are therefore recorded as figure only.
record.test_reason: The study directly measures representational similarity and finds input-dependent, incomplete alignment, bearing on V6 and V7. Different pretraining-token counts alone do not test V1's relationship between model size, capability and alignment.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors report geographic patterns in transfer and CKA that depend on pretraining data volume, feasible but uneven MSA-to-dialect transfer, and evidence of negative interference for high-resource dialects in multi-dialect models. These are observational findings subject to model and data confounds.
record.recipe_differences: Uses CKA to compare representations, but applies it to BERT-style MSA and dialect encoders on parallel Arabic dialect data rather than testing broad cross-architecture, cross-objective convergence as models scale.
record.method_sensitivity: CKA similarity varies with the pairing of input varieties across the three scenarios; the paper also reports different model rankings across scenarios and a data-scale association.

fits_no_version.finding: Task probing shows uneven transfer and possible negative interference; DziriBERT's relatively high CKA does not ensure superior probing performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representational similarity need not predict downstream task usefulness or equitable cross-dialect transfer.

record.problems: CKA values are presented in figures without numerical values in the text; compared models differ in training size, vocabularies, and pretraining hyperparameters; the paper notes imperfect dialect identification and proxy NER annotation noise, and acknowledges that Yemen is an operational, non-definitive geographic anchor. Similarity comparisons use MADAR parallel sentences and do not test out-of-distribution inputs.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted; the CKA results for 10 dialect models across 3 scenarios are recorded separately. Probing F1 results were excluded because they measure task performance, not representational similarity.

untested.parts: No model-size or capability trend in representational alignment is measured. Associations with pretraining corpus size across heterogeneous encoders do not establish convergence as models become larger and more capable.
No vision-language comparison or paired images and captions.
No comparison across random initializations of the same architecture.
No representation mapping, stitching, relative representations or interchangeability evaluation. Separately trained task probes do not establish interchangeability.
No identification of recurring interpretable features or circuits.
Alternative similarity measures, metric settings and systematic out-of-distribution evaluation are untested; only input-variety and pairing dependence under linear CKA is tested.
No scaling plateau or causal test of shared data or objectives as explanations for alignment. Possible MSA contamination is acknowledged, not experimentally isolated.

record.verdict_notes: All CKA comparisons use CAMeLBERT-MSA as the reference. Token counts describe pretraining corpora, not parameter sizes. Exact figure values cannot be recovered from the supplied text, but Section 5.2 explicitly establishes the qualitative effects and the below-0.8 bound. CKA below 0.8 establishes incomplete alignment under this measure; it does not alone establish missing dialect-specific information or failed interchangeability. Scenario 3 changes input variety across encoders, so its decrease cannot be attributed solely to differences between the models.

versions.untested_parts: The study compares BERT-style encoders with different stated pretraining-token counts, but does not conduct a controlled parameter/compute scale sweep, measure capability as a function of scale, or compare different architectures, objectives, and modalities.
No vision-language models or image-caption pairs are studied.
The study does not compare models trained from different random initializations of the same architecture or test shared features/subspaces across seeds.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired interchangeability test is performed.
The study does not identify or compare recurring interpretable features, neurons, or circuits.

The paper varies the input scenario for CKA comparisons, but does not compare alternative similarity metrics or systematically vary metric settings such as neighbour count, nor test out-of-distribution inputs.

The study reports incomplete CKA alignment and discusses pretraining-data scale, but does not establish that shared training data or objectives cause alignment, or test whether alignment plateaus as models scale.
